passage: I'm Rekha, Charu's big sister, and I've noticed my sister has started doing a new thing. When she comes home from school, before she even takes off her shoes, she tells us everyone's marks. "Riddhi got 19, Bunty got 15, I got 17. So I'm third." Yesterday she won a medal in the drawing competition and bounced around the house all evening. Today she came home silent. When I asked, she said, "Anaya's drawing got put on the main board. Mine only went on the class board." Same drawing, same medal. She went from the happiest person in the house to someone sitting on the stairs pulling at her socks. I don't know what's going on inside her head. But I don't think it's the drawing she's measuring.

qa.q: What did Charu win yesterday?
qa.a: A medal in the drawing competition.

qa.q: Why might Charu have come home silent today, with the same medal?
qa.a: Seeing Anaya's drawing on the main board made her feel small, as if her worth depended on where she ranked.

qa.q: How could Rekha support Charu on the stairs?
qa.a: Rekha could sit with her and ask what she likes about her own drawing, drawing her attention back from the rankings to the work itself.

qa.q: How might Charu's parents feel hearing everyone's marks before her shoes are even off?
qa.a: They might be amused at first, then worried that Charu measures herself so much against others.

grounding: An older sister watches a child track classmates' marks and prizes, swinging between pride and feeling small depending on her rank.

passage:
Tuesday. The science tests came back. Tejas had 14 out of 20 and immediately craned to see Vinita's paper: 19. His ears went hot. He turned his paper face down and didn't speak at lunch.
Friday. At sports day, Tejas came first in the sack race. He counted: three medals for Vinita last year, one for him now. Still behind, he thought, but he walked a little taller.
The next Wednesday. Instead of only checking Vinita's mark, Tejas asked her how she'd answered the question about plant cells. "I draw it first, then label," she said, showing him. He tried it on the homework and got the diagram right. That evening, though, he still wrote in the back of his notebook: Vinita 19, me 14. He looked at it for a while, then drew a small plant cell next to it.

qa.q: What did Vinita score in the science test?
qa.a: 19 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Tejas feel on Tuesday after seeing Vinita's paper?
qa.a: He felt small and embarrassed, which is why his ears went hot and he turned his paper face down.

qa.q: Which choice on Wednesday turned comparing into something useful?
qa.a: Asking Vinita how she answered the plant-cell question and trying her method, so the comparison helped him learn.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Tejas asking about her method?
qa.a: Vinita might feel pleased and happy to help, unaware that Tejas had been keeping score of her marks.

grounding: Over a week a child ranks himself against a classmate, feeling small or proud, and begins to use the comparison to learn.

passage: Charu, you're upset because Meenu got more stars than you? Sit here with your Rekha nani. When I was ten, I kept a list in my head of every girl in my class: who wrote neater, who sang better, who had shinier shoes. When I came first, I walked home like a queen. When Sudha beat me in sums, I wouldn't eat my dinner. My mother used to say, "Rekha, you are only as happy as your last rank." It was true. Then one day our teacher put my old copy from the start of the year beside my new one. So much better! I hadn't even noticed, because I was only ever looking at Sudha. Looking at others can tell you where you are, beta. Just don't let it tell you who you are.

qa.q: What did young Rekha's teacher put side by side?
qa.a: Rekha's old copy from the start of the year and her new one.

qa.q: What did young Rekha feel when Sudha beat her in sums?
qa.a: She felt so small and upset that she wouldn't eat her dinner.

qa.q: What could Charu try, instead of counting Meenu's stars?
qa.a: Charu could compare today's work with earlier work, as Rekha nani's teacher showed her, to see real progress.

qa.q: How might Rekha nani's mother have felt watching her daughter's moods rise and fall with each rank?
qa.a: She probably worried, which is why she told Rekha she was only as happy as her last rank.

grounding: A grandmother recalls ranking herself against classmates as a child, her self-worth rising and falling with each comparison.

passage: The drawing competition was in a school hall so noisy with parents and loudspeakers that Gurleen could barely think. Twenty minutes left. Gurleen liked her river, until she glanced at Gopika's paper: a whole village, with tiny goats. Suddenly her river looked thin. She looked again. And again. Each time, Gopika's picture seemed better and hers worse. Ten minutes left, and only half her sky was coloured. Gopika won a certificate; Gurleen got nothing. On the way home she said, "I'm bad at drawing." Papa said, "Last week you told me you were the best in class." Gurleen thought. "That was when I only saw Nimmi's."

qa.q: How much time was left when Gurleen first glanced at Gopika's paper?
qa.a: Twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel each time she looked at Gopika's drawing?
qa.a: She felt smaller each time; Gopika's picture seemed better and hers worse, though she had liked her river before.

qa.q: What went wrong during the competition, and what could Gurleen try next time?
qa.a: Checking Gopika's paper again and again used up her time, so half the sky stayed blank; next time she could keep her eyes on her own river until the end.

qa.q: How might Papa see Gurleen's two opposite claims about her drawing?
qa.a: Papa can see that her opinion of herself swings with whoever she compares against, so the ranking, not the drawing, is shaping how she feels.

grounding: A child keeps checking a classmate's drawing during a noisy competition and feels smaller each time, showing how constant ranking colours self-worth.

passage: In the Pune housing society's skating class, every child had a sticker chart. Mahima checked everyone's before she even tied her skates. Eshaan: four stickers. Hers: six. She skated faster that evening, grinning. On Thursday a new girl, Sia, arrived with ten stickers from her old class. Mahima's legs felt heavy. She fell twice and told the coach she had a tummy ache. Walking home past the vegetable carts, Eshaan asked, "Why are you sad? You learnt the turn today." Mahima blinked. She had forgotten the turn completely. "I did, na?" She tried it again on the society path, wobbling, and laughed.

qa.q: How many stickers did Sia have?
qa.a: Ten stickers, from her old class.

qa.q: Why did Mahima tell the coach she had a tummy ache?
qa.a: She felt small and deflated after seeing Sia's ten stickers, and wanted a way out of skating while she felt like that.

qa.q: What turning point did Eshaan's question create for Mahima?
qa.a: By reminding her she learnt the turn today, Eshaan helped her notice her own progress instead of the sticker count, and she happily tried it again 🙂

qa.q: How might Eshaan feel about being counted against Mahima's chart?
qa.a: With four stickers, Eshaan might feel ranked below her, yet he still noticed her progress kindly, which suggests he wasn't keeping score the same way.

grounding: A child ranks friends by skating stickers and feels proud or small by turns, until a friend's question points her back to her own progress.
